strengths: The core idea—reformulating standard SSL pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, patch position) as verifiable RL rewards for VLM post-training—is a clean and practical way to avoid human preference data or LLM-as-judge signals, and is a useful reframing even though the underlying tasks are well known.

Broad empirical coverage: vision-centric (ImageNet) and vision-language reasoning (MMBench, SEED-Bench) benchmarks at two model scales (3B/7B), plus a genuinely distinct extension to graph-structured data with three SSL tasks, showing the framework is not narrowly tailored to one modality.

Systematic ablations on task difficulty, model-size scaling, and task combination provide some actionable design heuristics ("difficulty must match model capacity", non-additivity of naively combined rewards) that could be useful starting points for follow-up work.

Reasonably transparent reporting: full per-dimension results in the appendix, training curves, and qualitative case studies (attention maps, example transcripts) that attempt to explain why gains occur (sharper visual grounding, reduced linguistic-prior reliance).
Reproducibility details (hyperparameters, GRPO configuration, evaluation toolkit) are provided, and the authors commit to releasing code.
weaknesses: Missing critical control experiments: there is no baseline that applies GRPO/RL with a verifiable but semantically irrelevant reward (e.g., arbitrary classification or formatting-compliance reward) to isolate whether gains stem from SSL task semantics specifically or simply from generic RL post-training that improves instruction-following/output formatting on multiple-choice benchmarks. Given the very large jumps reported (e.g., +39 points on MMBench Relation Reasoning from a rotation-prediction reward), this confound is plausible and not ruled out.

The mechanistic explanations offered (e.g., rotation prediction as "anti-commonsense learning," contrastive task "too easy" hence weak) are post-hoc narratives supported mainly by 2-3 qualitative attention-map examples rather than systematic, quantitative evidence (e.g., attention entropy/IoU statistics across a larger sample, ablations directly testing the causal claims).

No variance/robustness reporting: single-run numbers are given throughout without seeds, error bars, or statistical significance testing, which is important given how large and sometimes non-monotonic (e.g., task combination underperforming best single task) the reported effects are.

The task-combination experiment shows no improvement over single-task training, weakening the generality/robustness narrative, and the explanation for this remains speculative without further diagnostic experiments (e.g., examining gradient conflict directly).
Minor inconsistencies between reported average improvements in the abstract (9%/8%) and in the main text (7.39%/8.94%) suggest limited care in number reporting, which raises reproducibility concerns.

The graph extension applies a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) to text-attributed graph tasks without clear justification of why a vision-language model (rather than a text-only LLM or a GNN) is the appropriate backbone for this domain, making the "generalization to graph" claim somewhat orthogonal to the paper's main vision-language motivation and harder to interpret.

No comparison to alternative post-training baselines (e.g., RLHF/DPO with human/AI preference data, or straightforward SFT/RL directly on downstream VQA data) that would contextualize how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific SSL-derived rewards versus simply doing additional RL fine-tuning at all.

Limited discussion of reward hacking or degenerate solutions in the SSL4RL rewards (e.g., models exploiting superficial cues to solve rotation/jigsaw without learning transferable visual grounding), despite this being a central risk in reward-shaping approaches.

strengths: Broad and systematic empirical study: the paper evaluates SSL4RL across many benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet-1K, V*, RealWorldQA, BLINK, MME-RealWorld-Lite, CapArena), two model families (Qwen2.5-VL, Gemma3) at two scales (3B/7B), and even extends the idea to graph learning with three SSL tasks—providing a comprehensive picture of when the paradigm helps.

The core idea—reformulating self-supervised pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, patch position) as intrinsically verifiable RL rewards for VLM post-training—is a clean, practically useful contribution that avoids reliance on human preference data or LLM-as-judge signals for most of the training pipeline.

Extensive and thoughtful ablations (data volume scaling, model size scaling, task difficulty scaling, task combination, base model choice, robustness to perturbations) go beyond a single positive result and try to extract general design principles ('Goldilocks difficulty', capacity-task alignment, non-additivity of combined rewards).

The comparison against an oracle 'Golden-3B' baseline trained with task-specific golden-answer rewards is a valuable and rigorous way to contextualize how much of the achievable gain SSL4RL can capture without labels.

Qualitative analyses (attention heatmaps, case studies showing reduced reliance on linguistic priors) provide some mechanistic insight into why the method helps, complementing the quantitative results.

The paper is transparent about negative/mixed findings (e.g., contrastive learning underperforming without stronger augmentation, diminishing returns at 7B scale, non-additive task combination), which strengthens the credibility of the analysis rather than only reporting favorable results.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to acknowledged concurrent/prior work (Jigsaw-R1, Spatial-SSRL): the paper's core mechanism (corrupt image, get verifiable reward, apply GRPO) is essentially a generalization of ideas already published, and the paper does not provide a head-to-head quantitative comparison against these closely related methods.

Reported gains are very large in places (e.g., +39 points on MMBench Relation Reasoning, near-chance base-model accuracy on seemingly simple rotation prediction), which raises questions about whether the base-model baseline evaluation (prompting/parsing, zero-shot instruction format) is fully fair, especially since these effects are not cross-validated with alternative baselines or multiple seeds/runs; no variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-trial statistics are reported anywhere in the paper.

The open-ended captioning evaluation relies on GPT-4o as a judge (CapArena), which is philosophically in tension with the paper's stated motivation of avoiding 'unreliable AI evaluators'; results in this section are also somewhat noisy/non-monotonic (e.g., Position task gives 0.00 GPT-Score in two of the settings, underperforming even the base model on that sub-metric), undermining the claimed generality of the approach for open-ended tasks.

Model-size scaling study is based on only two points (3B and 7B) plus a single alternative architecture (Gemma3-4B) at reduced batch size, which is a fairly narrow basis for the strong claims made about a general 'capacity-task difficulty matching' principle and 'diminishing returns' trend.

All experiments use an identical fixed GRPO configuration across very different SSL tasks and domains (vision, graph); it is unclear whether this represents a fair comparison, since different reward structures (e.g., binary contrastive vs. multi-class rotation) may need different learning rates, KL coefficients, or group sizes to reach their full potential, potentially confounding the difficulty/task-comparison conclusions.

Several explanatory narratives (e.g., rotation prediction as 'anti-commonsense learning', qualitative attention-sharpening claims) are plausible but only supported by a handful of cherry-picked qualitative examples rather than systematic, quantitative validation.

Minor presentation issues: the abstract references an empty code/model URL, and some appendix tables (e.g., graph 7B results, CapArena scores) show non-monotonic or counterintuitive patterns that are not fully discussed or reconciled with the main narrative.
